about: Help text for every setting. The Python prototype and the C++ plugin both use this file, so the text is written only once. 'short' is one line (for a status bar). 'tooltip' is the detailed text shown when the mouse is over a control. 'default' must match the code. 'min'/'max' are the knob range in the plugin.

preset.label: Preset
preset.short: One complete amp: a list of blocks that run from top to bottom.
preset.tooltip: A preset is one whole amp. It is a list of blocks (EQ, gain stage, sag, feedback, cab IR) that the sound goes through from top to bottom. You can put the blocks in any order and use each kind as many times as you like. Every amp ever built can be described this way: some tone shaping, some clipping, a power supply that sags, and a feedback loop.

name.label: Name
name.tooltip: The name shown in the preset list. It does not change the sound.

notes.label: Notes
notes.short: Your own notes about this amp.
notes.tooltip: Free text for yourself: what the amp is meant to sound like, which guitar it suits, what you changed. It does not change the sound.

chain.label: Chain
chain.short: The blocks of the amp, in the order the sound goes through them.
chain.tooltip: The order matters a lot. EQ before a gain stage changes WHAT gets clipped (cut the bass before the clipping for a tight sound; boost the mids before it for a singing lead). EQ after a gain stage only changes the TONE of the clipped sound, like the tone knobs on a real amp. Put the cab IR last.

type.label: Block type

choices.tonestack: The real bass/mid/treble circuit of a tube amp, worked out from its part values.
choices.gain: One gain stage: filter, clip, filter.
choices.sag: Power supply sag: lowers the clipping ceiling of later gain stages when you play hard.
choices.feedback: A loop around a few blocks, like the feedback loop of a power amp.
choices.split: Parallel paths: the same sound goes through several chains side by side, then they are mixed.
choices.gate: Noise gate: turns the sound down when you stop playing, to remove hiss and hum.
choices.ir: Speaker cabinet sound from an impulse response file.

type.short: What kind of block this is.
type.tooltip: Each block does one job. Combine them in any order to build any amp.

id.label: Name (id)
id.short: A short name for this block, so other blocks can point to it.
id.tooltip: Optional. Give a block an id (for example "power") when a sag block must control it. Each id must be used only once in a preset. It does not change the sound.

band.label: Filter band
band.short: One filter: boosts or cuts a range of tones.
band.tooltip: A filter band is the basic tool for shaping tone. It is used inside EQ blocks, before and after the clipping in gain stages, and in the path of a feedback loop. Several bands in a row add up.

kind.label: Type

choices.highpass: Removes everything BELOW the frequency. Use it to remove mud and boom. 'freq' is where the cut starts; 'q' sets how sharp the corner is.
choices.lowpass: Removes everything ABOVE the frequency. Use it to remove fizz and harshness. 'freq' is where the cut starts; 'q' sets how sharp the corner is.
choices.lowshelf: Raises or lowers everything below the frequency by the same amount, like a bass knob. 'gain_db' sets how much.
choices.highshelf: Raises or lowers everything above the frequency by the same amount, like a treble knob. 'gain_db' sets how much.
choices.peak: Raises or lowers a range of tones around the frequency, like one band of a parametric EQ. 'q' sets how wide the range is.

kind.tooltip: High-pass and low-pass remove tones. Shelves work like the bass and treble knobs on a hi-fi. Peak changes one area in the middle, like a parametric EQ.

freq.label: Frequency
freq.short: Which tones this band works on.
freq.tooltip: The pitch where the filter acts. Rough guide for guitar: 80-150 Hz = boom and body, 200-400 Hz = warmth or mud, 500-1000 Hz = the 'honk' and the voice of the amp, 1-3 kHz = bite and cutting through a band, 3-6 kHz = presence and pick attack, above 6 kHz = fizz and air. A guitar speaker plays almost nothing above about 5-6 kHz.

q.label: Width (Q)
q.short: How narrow the band is. Higher = narrower.
q.tooltip: For 'peak': a low Q (0.5-1) changes a wide area and sounds natural; a high Q (4-10) hits a small area, good for removing one ugly ring. For high-pass, low-pass and shelves: 0.707 gives a smooth corner with no bump; higher values add a bump right at the corner frequency (the old amp circuits often have such a bump).

gain_db.label: Boost / cut
gain_db.short: How much to raise (+) or lower (-) the tones. Used by shelves and peaks.
gain_db.tooltip: +6 dB is about twice as loud in that area; -6 dB is about half. Small changes (2-4 dB) are often enough. Big boosts before a gain stage make that area clip much more, which changes the character of the distortion, not only the tone. High-pass and low-pass ignore this setting.

split_path.label: Split path
split_path.short: One of the parallel chains inside a split block.
split_path.tooltip: Each path gets the same input. Its own chain of blocks runs on it, then it is mixed with the other paths at its own level.

chain.label: Chain
chain.short: The blocks in this path. Empty = the untouched input.
chain.tooltip: Any blocks can go here, even another split, a feedback loop or a cab IR. Leave it empty to pass the input through untouched: useful for a clean blend under a distorted path.

level_db.label: Level
level_db.short: How loud this path is in the mix.
level_db.tooltip: Works like the volume knob of one channel in a 'jumpered' amp: turn one path down to hear more of the other. -60 dB is about off. Since paths are simply added, the total gets louder when several paths are up; use the split block's Level to bring it back.

invert.label: Invert
invert.short: Flips this path upside down before mixing (polarity).
invert.tooltip: When two paths are mixed and one is flipped, the tones they share cancel out and only the differences stay. Real circuits do this: some tube stages flip the signal and some do not, so two paths through a different number of stages can partly cancel. Try it when a blend sounds thin or hollow: flipping one path often fixes it (or makes it the special sound you want). Two identical paths with one flipped = silence.

tonestack.label: Tone stack
tonestack.short: The real bass/mid/treble circuit of a tube amp, worked out from its part values.
tonestack.tooltip: Almost every famous tube amp uses the same passive tone circuit (3 capacitors, 1 resistor, 3 pots), only with different part values. This block works out that exact circuit, so the knobs behave like the real amp: they affect each other (for example, Mid also changes the treble level), there is a built-in mid scoop, and the whole circuit loses volume, as in the real amp. Checked against the published formula for this circuit (Yeh and Smith, 2006): same answer within 0.001 dB. Where to put it: after the first one or two gain stages in most British and American amps; BEFORE the gain stages in some amps (for example the Mesa Mark series), which makes the knobs change the distortion itself.

style.label: Part values

choices.british: Values like the classic British 100 W amps: C1 470 pF, C2 22 nF, C3 22 nF, treble 220k, bass 1M, mid 25k, slope 33k. Less mid scoop (about -5 dB at 700 Hz with all knobs at 5), punchy mids.
choices.american: Values like the 1959 American tweed bass amp (the circuit the British amps copied): C1 250 pF, C2 20 nF, C3 20 nF, treble 250k, bass 1M, mid 25k, slope 56k. Deeper mid scoop (about -7 dB at 760 Hz with all knobs at 5).

style.short: Which set of part values to start from.
style.tooltip: The starting part values. Any single part can then be changed with 'Parts'. The values are from common published schematics; check them against the schematic of the exact amp you want to copy.

parts.label: Parts

names.C1: Treble capacitor (farads, e.g. 470e-12 = 470 pF). Bigger = the treble knob reaches lower and the sound gets brighter.
names.C2: Bass capacitor (farads, e.g. 22e-9 = 22 nF). Bigger = more low bass.
names.C3: Mid capacitor (farads). Bigger = the mid knob works lower.
names.R2: Bass pot total resistance (ohms). Bigger = more bass range.
names.R3: Mid pot total resistance (ohms). Bigger = more mids overall.
names.R4: Slope resistor (ohms). The most important value for the character: smaller = more mids and more output (British), bigger = deeper scoop (American, and amps with a 100k slope resistor sound very scooped).

parts.short: Change any single part value of the circuit.
parts.tooltip: Only list the parts you want to change; the others come from the style. Units are farads and ohms: 470 pF = 470e-12, 22 nF = 22e-9, 220k = 220e3, 1M = 1e6. This is how you copy one exact amp from its schematic.

treble.label: Treble
treble.tooltip: Moves the output pick-off point along the treble pot. Up = more highs, AND less mids and bass (the knobs share one circuit). Measured with British values and the other knobs at 5: 3 kHz goes from -10.5 dB (treble 0) to -1.7 dB (treble 10).

mid.label: Middle
mid.tooltip: Sets how much the mid pot holds the mids up. Up = more mids AND a louder sound overall, because more of the signal gets through. At 0 you get the deepest scoop and the lowest volume. Measured with British values: 500 Hz goes from -11.8 dB (mid 0) to -6.6 dB (mid 10), and 3 kHz moves too (-8.5 to -4.1 dB).

bass.label: Bass
bass.tooltip: Sets how much low end gets through. Most of the change happens in the top half of the knob when the taper is 'log' (like the real audio-taper pot). Measured with British values: 100 Hz goes from -10.7 dB (bass 0) to -2.7 dB (bass 10). The effect is a bit smaller when the treble is high, because the knobs share one circuit.

treble_taper.label: Treble taper

choices.linear: Resistance changes evenly as you turn.
choices.log: Audio taper: at the half-way point only 10% of the resistance. Most of the change is at the top of the knob.

treble_taper.short: How the treble pot's resistance changes as you turn it.
treble_taper.tooltip: Real amps use either kind; the schematic says 'LIN' (linear, sometimes 'B') or 'LOG' (audio, sometimes 'A'). It changes where on the knob the sound changes most, not the range.

mid_taper.label: Middle taper

choices.linear: Resistance changes evenly as you turn.
choices.log: Audio taper: at the half-way point only 10% of the resistance.

mid_taper.short: How the mid pot's resistance changes as you turn it.
mid_taper.tooltip: See Treble taper. Check the schematic of the amp you copy.

bass_taper.label: Bass taper

choices.linear: Resistance changes evenly as you turn.
choices.log: Audio taper: at the half-way point only 10% of the resistance (the usual choice for bass pots).

bass_taper.short: How the bass pot's resistance changes as you turn it.
bass_taper.tooltip: See Treble taper. Bass pots are usually audio taper ('LOG' or 'A').

source_ohms.label: Source resistance
source_ohms.short: The output resistance of the tube stage that drives the tone stack.
source_ohms.tooltip: A cathode follower (most British and high-gain amps, and the 1959 tweed bass amp) drives the tone stack with about 1k: use 1000. A normal tube stage drives it from its plate, with roughly 30k-40k: the stack then loses more highs and the knobs behave differently (American 'blackface'-style amps). This setting copies that.

load_ohms.label: Load resistance
load_ohms.short: The resistance after the tone stack (usually the next tube's grid resistor or volume pot).
load_ohms.tooltip: Usually a 1M volume pot or grid resistor: use 1e6. A smaller load (for example a 250k volume pot) takes away some low end and volume.

level_db.label: Level
level_db.tooltip: The tone stack loses about 5-20 dB like the real circuit (the stage after it in a real amp makes up for it). Raise this, or the drive of the next gain stage, to get the level back.

gate.label: Noise gate
gate.short: Turns the sound down when you stop playing, to remove hiss and hum.
gate.tooltip: High-gain amps make the small hiss and hum of a guitar very loud. The gate follows the signal level: when it falls below the threshold, the gate closes and turns the sound down; when you play again, it opens. Best use: put the gate at the START of the chain (where the guitar signal is clean and the hiss is quiet) and set 'Apply after' to the last gain stage (where the hiss is loud). Then the gate decides on the clean signal but mutes the loud hiss. A gate placed after a high-gain amp hears the amplified hiss as 'playing' and may never close.

threshold_db.label: Threshold
threshold_db.short: The gate opens when the signal is louder than this.
threshold_db.tooltip: Set it above the PEAKS of the hiss when you are not playing. Hiss peaks are about 10 dB above its average level, so hiss that measures -70 dB needs a threshold of about -55 dB. Too low: the gate stays open and the hiss gets through. Too high: quiet notes and the ends of ringing notes get cut off. At the start of the chain, typical values are -60 to -40 dB. Listen to the end of a ringing chord while you set it. The level the gate follows is the biggest peak in the last 20 ms, so it does not flicker between the peaks of a low note.

hysteresis_db.label: Hysteresis
hysteresis_db.short: The gate closes this many dB BELOW the threshold, so it does not flutter.
hysteresis_db.tooltip: A note that fades out slowly sits near the threshold for a while. If opening and closing happened at the same level, the gate would flutter open and shut ('chatter'). With 6 dB, the gate opens at the threshold but only closes when the level is 6 dB lower. Important: the closing point (threshold minus hysteresis) must still be above the hiss peaks, or the gate never closes. Measured with hiss at -70 dB and threshold -55 dB: 0 dB = the gate fluttered 4-8 times on one fading note; 3 dB = it opened once and closed once (clean); 6 dB = it never closed, because the closing point (-61 dB) was under the hiss peaks. If the gate does not close, lower this or raise the threshold.

attack_ms.label: Attack
attack_ms.short: How fast the gate opens when you play.
attack_ms.tooltip: Keep it very short (0.1-1 ms) so the pick attack is not lost. Longer values soften the start of every note, which can be a special effect (a 'swell').

hold_ms.label: Hold
hold_ms.short: How long the gate waits before closing.
hold_ms.tooltip: After the level falls below the closing point, the gate stays open for this long. It stops the gate from closing in the short gaps inside fast riffs. For tight staccato metal riffs: 10-30 ms. For normal playing: 50-150 ms.

release_ms.label: Release
release_ms.tooltip: Short (5-30 ms): very tight cut-offs for modern high-gain riffs, but ringing notes can end abruptly. Long (100-500 ms): notes fade out naturally, the hiss fades with them.

range_db.label: Range
range_db.short: How much the sound is turned down when the gate is closed.
range_db.tooltip: -80 dB = fully silent. -20 to -10 dB = the hiss is only made quieter, which sounds more natural, because a fully silent gate can make the starts and ends of notes stand out.

apply_after.label: Apply after
apply_after.short: Optional: the id of a later block. The gate listens here but mutes after that block.
apply_after.tooltip: Leave empty to gate the sound right here. Set it to the id of a later block (for example the last gain stage) to listen to the clean signal here but mute the loud hiss after that block. The sound passes through the gate's own position unchanged. The block must come after the gate and can not be inside a feedback loop (use the feedback block's own id instead).

split.label: Split
split.short: Parallel paths: the same sound goes through several chains side by side, then they are mixed.
split.tooltip: Lets an amp have more than one path. Examples: the 'jumpered' channels of old British amps (a bright channel and a normal channel mixed, each with its own volume); a clean signal blended under a high-gain sound to keep the pick attack; two cab IRs (or two microphones) mixed; a bass path and a treble path with different gain. Each path can hold any blocks.

paths.label: Paths
paths.short: The parallel chains. At least one.
paths.tooltip: Each path has its own chain, level and invert switch. All paths get the same input, and their outputs are added together.

level_db.label: Level
level_db.short: Volume after the paths are mixed.
level_db.tooltip: Adding paths together makes the sound louder (two equal paths = +6 dB). Use this to bring the level back, or to set how hard the mix drives the next gain stage.

eq.label: EQ
eq.short: Tone shaping with a list of filter bands.
eq.tooltip: Shapes the tone with any number of filter bands. Before a gain stage it decides which tones get clipped hardest. After a gain stage it works like the tone knobs of an amp. EQ adds no delay and no distortion.

bands.label: Bands
bands.short: The filter bands, applied one after another.
bands.tooltip: Add as many bands as you need. Each one is a high-pass, low-pass, low shelf, high shelf or peak. With no bands, the EQ only changes the level.

level_db.label: Level
level_db.tooltip: Raises or lowers the volume of everything that comes out of this block. If the next block is a gain stage, this works like a gain knob: more level = more clipping in that stage.

gain.label: Gain stage
gain.short: One tube-like stage: filter, then drive into a clipping curve, then filter.
gain.tooltip: This is where the distortion happens. The sound goes: pre filters, then Drive pushes it into the clipping curve, then post filters, then Level. One stage with low drive = clean or edge of breakup. Two or three stages in a row with EQ between them = classic high-gain amps. The clipping is done at a higher sample rate (oversampling) so it does not sound harsh or fizzy.

drive_db.label: Drive
drive_db.short: How hard the sound hits the clipping curve. More = more distortion.
drive_db.tooltip: The main gain knob of this stage. At 0 dB, a normal guitar signal stays almost clean. Around +12 dB: crunch. Around +24 dB: classic rock lead. +36 dB and more: high gain. More drive also means more compression: soft and loud notes come out closer in volume. Very high drive on one stage sounds fizzy; spreading the gain over several stages (with EQ between them) usually sounds better.

curve.label: Clipping curve

choices.soft: Smooth, round clipping (tanh). Warm and natural, both sides the same. Only odd harmonics. A safe start for any stage.
choices.tube: Uneven like a real triode: the top clips earlier and harder than the bottom. Adds even harmonics, which sound thicker and sweeter. Best for preamp stages.
choices.diode: Stays clean longer, then bends quickly. Sounds like a pedal with clipping diodes: tighter and more compressed than 'soft'.
choices.hard: Flat cut at the ceiling. Buzzy and aggressive, like a fuzz or a broken transistor. Best used with a low-pass after it.
choices.custom: Set the top and the bottom of the wave separately: where each side clips and how soft the bend is. Use it to copy a cathode follower (only the top clips), a pedal with uneven diodes, a fuzz, or anything else.
choices.triode: A real preamp tube (12AX7, 12AT7 or 12AU7) worked out from published tube equations, with its supply voltage, plate resistor and bias. The input is in volts at the grid. Small signals get mostly 2nd harmonic (the classic tube warmth); the top clips hard where grid current starts, the bottom squashes gradually toward cut-off.

curve.short: The shape of the clipping. Changes the character of the distortion.
curve.tooltip: All curves pass small signals unchanged and squash big ones. They differ in HOW they squash: soft and tube bend gradually (warm), diode bends late and fast (tight), hard cuts flat (buzzy). Uneven curves (tube, triode, custom with different sides, or any curve with Bias) add even harmonics. Measured with a 220 Hz note: soft = 0% 2nd and 6.7% 3rd harmonic; triode 12AX7 at 0.5 V = 2.6% 2nd and 0.1% 3rd; triode biased cold (-2.5 V) at 2 V = 24% 2nd harmonic.

top.label: Top level
top.short: Custom curve: where the top half of the wave clips.
top.tooltip: The highest level the top half of the wave can reach. Smaller = the top clips sooner. Making top and bottom different gives even harmonics (a thicker, more 'tube' sound). Example: a cathode follower clips only the top: top 1, bottom 20. Only used when Curve is 'custom'.

top_softness.label: Top softness
top_softness.short: Custom curve: how soft the top bend is. 0 = almost a hard corner, 1 = very gradual.
top_softness.tooltip: 0 = stays clean almost up to the level and then cuts nearly flat (diode-like, buzzy). 0.5 = a round bend, similar to a tube. 1 = starts squashing early and very gradually (smooth, compressed). Measured: at an input equal to the level, the output is 92% (softness 0), 78% (0.5), 50% (1) of the level. Only used when Curve is 'custom'.

bottom.label: Bottom level
bottom.short: Custom curve: where the bottom half of the wave clips.
bottom.tooltip: The lowest level the bottom half of the wave can reach (as a positive number). See Top level. Only used when Curve is 'custom'.

bottom_softness.label: Bottom softness
bottom_softness.short: Custom curve: how soft the bottom bend is.
bottom_softness.tooltip: See Top softness. Only used when Curve is 'custom'.

tube.label: Tube

choices.12AX7: The usual preamp tube: high gain (about 60 per stage with a 100k plate resistor). Used in almost every guitar amp preamp.
choices.12AT7: Medium gain (about 45). Often used in reverb drivers and phase inverters; cleaner and stiffer in a preamp.
choices.12AU7: Low gain (about 15). Lots of headroom; very clean. Used as a gentle first stage or a cathode follower.

tube.tooltip: Each tube has its own gain and curve shape. The numbers come from Koren's tube models (1996), which are widely used in tube simulation. Only used when Curve is 'triode'.

plate_v.label: Supply voltage
plate_v.short: Triode curve: the supply voltage at the top of the plate resistor.
plate_v.tooltip: Higher = more headroom, cleaner and louder. Lower = 'starved', clips sooner and more unevenly. Typical preamp supplies are 200-350 V. Measured: a 12AX7 with 100k and -1.5 V bias sits at 205 V on the plate with 300 V supply (about 1 mA, gain 61), like the real tube. Only used when Curve is 'triode'.

plate_ohms.label: Plate resistor
plate_ohms.short: Triode curve: the plate resistor (the stage's load).
plate_ohms.tooltip: 100k is the usual value. A bigger plate resistor gives a bit more gain and clips sooner; a smaller one gives more headroom. Copy it from the schematic (usually written like '100K' next to the tube's plate). Only used when Curve is 'triode'.

bias_v.label: Bias voltage
bias_v.short: Triode curve: the grid voltage at rest (below 0). Sets how 'hot' or 'cold' the stage is.
bias_v.tooltip: The most important setting for the character of a tube stage. Around -1 to -1.5 V (a 1.5k cathode resistor in a real amp) = a normal 'hot' stage: the top clips first when the grid reaches 0 V (grid current). Around -2.5 to -4 V (a 10k cathode resistor) = a 'cold clipper': the bottom squashes very early, which gives a lot of 2nd harmonic and the tight, aggressive grind of many high-gain amps (measured: 24% 2nd harmonic at -2.5 V). In a real amp, bias voltage = cathode current x cathode resistor. Only used when Curve is 'triode'. With this curve, Drive sets how many volts reach the grid: a guitar gives about 0.1-1 V, earlier stages give many volts.

bias.label: Bias
bias.short: Moves the clipping point off center, so one side of the wave clips before the other.
bias.tooltip: At 0 both sides clip the same. Moving it away from 0 makes one side clip first, which adds even harmonics (a thicker, warmer, more 'tube' sound) and makes the distortion change as notes fade out. Small values (0.05-0.2) are subtle. Large values give a gated, sputtering 'cold' sound like a starved tube or a dying battery. The DC offset this creates is removed automatically.

bias_shift.label: Bias shift
bias_shift.short: How much a loud signal pushes the stage 'colder' for a moment. 0 = off.
bias_shift.tooltip: In a real tube stage, a signal that goes past the top of the curve makes the grid draw current. This charges the capacitor in front of the tube and moves its working point down (colder). After the loud part, it drifts back. You hear it as: right after a hard hit, soft notes come out quieter, thinner and a bit sputtery, then they 'open up' again. This is a big part of how cascaded high-gain amps feel and why they 'chug'. Measured with 1.0: a soft note right after a loud chord came out 35% quieter with 5 times more 2nd harmonic, and was back to normal after about 100 ms. 0 = off (a stiff, 'perfect' stage). 0.3-0.6 = a normal tube stage. 1.0 = strong, gated, 'farty' blocking when hit very hard. Works with any curve; it only does something when the stage is driven past the top of the curve.

shift_attack_ms.label: Shift attack
shift_attack_ms.short: How fast the working point moves when hit hard.
shift_attack_ms.tooltip: In a real stage the capacitor charges fast, through the low resistance of the conducting grid: around 0.5-2 ms. Shorter = the pick attack itself gets squashed. Longer = the first hit gets through, then the stage chokes. Only matters when Bias shift is above 0.

shift_release_ms.label: Shift release
shift_release_ms.short: How fast the working point comes back after a loud part.
shift_release_ms.tooltip: In a real stage this is the coupling capacitor draining through the grid resistor (for example 22 nF x 1 Mohm = 22 ms). Short (10-30 ms): the stage recovers between notes; tight and fast. Long (100-500 ms): the stage stays choked after a hard hit; you hear a 'swell' as it recovers, and with fast palm mutes it sounds gated. Bigger coupling capacitors in a real amp = longer release. Only matters when Bias shift is above 0.

level_db.label: Level
level_db.tooltip: Sets the output volume of this stage. Since the clipping curve already limits the peaks, Level is how you set how hard this stage drives the NEXT stage. It works like the coupling between two tubes.

pre.label: Pre filters
pre.short: Filters before the clipping. They decide what gets distorted.
pre.tooltip: This is the most powerful tone control in an amp. Cutting bass before the clipping (high-pass at 100-700 Hz) gives a tight, clear distortion that does not get muddy, like the small coupling capacitors in real preamps. Boosting mids before the clipping (peak at 700-1000 Hz) gives a singing, pushed-amp lead tone. Real tube stages often have a gentle high-shelf boost here (the 'bright cap').

post.label: Post filters
post.short: Filters after the clipping. They smooth the distorted sound.
post.tooltip: A low-pass after the clipping (5-10 kHz) removes fizz, like the natural top-end loss of real tube stages. A 10 Hz high-pass is always added at the end to remove DC offset; you do not need to add it.

oversample.label: Oversampling

choices.1: Off. Fastest. Harsh fold-back noise with heavy clipping.
choices.16: 16x. Only for extreme high gain with the 'hard' curve.

oversample.short: How many times faster the clipping runs, to avoid harsh noise.
oversample.tooltip: Clipping creates very high tones. Without oversampling, the ones above the top of the sample rate fold back down as harsh, out-of-tune noise (aliasing). Measured with hard clipping at 4.5 kHz: off = noise only 21 dB below the sound, 8x = 62 dB below (not audible). Python prototype only: in the plugin the whole amp is oversampled once, so this setting will not be there.

sag.label: Sag
sag.short: Power supply sag: playing hard lowers the clipping ceiling of other stages for a moment.
sag.tooltip: In a real tube amp, playing hard pulls current from the power supply, so its voltage drops for a moment and the tubes clip earlier. This gives the soft, 'squishy', touch-sensitive feel of old amps, and the 'bloom' when a chord rings out and the supply recovers. The sag block listens to the sound where it sits (the sound passes through unchanged) and lowers the ceiling of the gain stages listed in Targets. Usually placed right before the power amp stage.

amount.label: Amount
amount.short: How far the ceiling can drop. 0 = no sag, 0.5 = down to half.
amount.tooltip: 0 = a stiff modern supply (tight, punchy, solid-state rectifier). 0.2-0.3 = a normal tube amp. 0.4-0.6 = a vintage tube-rectified amp: very squishy and compressed, the note 'blooms' after the pick attack. Above 0.6 the sound pumps and breathes with your playing. Quiet playing is not changed at all, only playing that reaches the ceiling.

sens_db.label: Sensitivity
sens_db.short: How easily the sag reacts. Higher = reacts to softer playing.
sens_db.tooltip: Raises or lowers the signal the sag listens to (the sound itself is not changed). If the sag only kicks in on the very hardest hits, raise it. If even light playing makes the sound squash, lower it. The right value depends on how loud the signal is where the sag block sits.

attack_ms.label: Attack
attack_ms.short: How fast the ceiling drops when you hit hard.
attack_ms.tooltip: Short (1-5 ms): the sag grabs right away, and the pick attack gets squashed too. Longer (10-30 ms): the first hit gets through at full punch, then the note settles and compresses. Real amps are around 2-10 ms.

release_ms.label: Release
release_ms.short: How fast the ceiling comes back when you play softer.
release_ms.tooltip: This is how fast the power supply recovers. Short (50-100 ms): tight, follows fast playing. Medium (150-300 ms): the classic 'bloom', where a ringing chord slowly opens up as the supply recovers. Long (500 ms and more): the amp stays compressed for a while after a hard hit, and can 'pump' with the rhythm.

targets.label: Targets
targets.short: The ids of the gain stages this sag controls.
targets.tooltip: List the gain stages that share this power supply. They must come after the sag block in the chain (a gain stage inside a later feedback block is fine). Usually the power amp stage. Adding preamp stages too gives an even softer, more 'saggy' feel.

feedback.label: Feedback loop
feedback.short: A loop around a few blocks: part of the output is sent back and taken away from the input.
feedback.tooltip: Most tube power amps send part of the speaker signal back to an earlier stage (negative feedback). This lowers the gain, makes the clipping cleaner and tighter, tightens the bass, and makes the amp sound less raw. Amps with little or no feedback sound loose, raw and aggressive; amps with a lot sound tight, clean and polished. The filters in Path decide which tones get less feedback, so those come out louder: that is how Presence and Resonance knobs work. Put the power amp gain stage (and its EQ) inside the loop.

amount.label: Amount
amount.short: How much of the output is fed back. More = tighter, cleaner, less gain.
amount.tooltip: 0 = no feedback (raw, loose, like amps that have none). Small values (0.1-0.3) = most classic amps. Larger values = tight and polished, the clipping becomes harder at the edge (clean, then suddenly clipped). The gain drops as amount goes up, so raise the drive of the inner stages or the level to make up for it. Note: the effect also depends on the inner gain; the real loop gain is about amount x the gain of the inner chain.

path.label: Path filters
path.short: Filters on the feedback signal. Tones they cut get less feedback, so they come out LOUDER.
path.tooltip: This works the opposite way to a normal EQ: cutting a tone here makes it louder at the output, because that tone is no longer held back by the feedback. Presence: high shelf around 2-4 kHz with -6 to -12 dB = more bite and sparkle. Resonance (or Depth): low shelf around 80-120 Hz with a cut = bigger, looser bass, like a closed-back cab pushing back. With no filters, all tones get the same feedback.

chain.label: Inside the loop
chain.short: The blocks inside the loop (EQ, tone stack and gain stages only).
chain.tooltip: Usually the power amp stage, maybe with an EQ for the output transformer (a high-pass around 60-100 Hz and a low-pass around 5-8 kHz). Inner gain stages can not set their own oversampling: the whole loop runs at the loop's oversampling rate.

oversample.label: Oversampling

choices.1: Off. Fastest, harsh with heavy clipping.

oversample.short: How many times faster the whole loop runs.
oversample.tooltip: Same idea as in the gain stage: it keeps clipping inside the loop from making harsh noise. In the Python prototype the loop is computed one sample at a time, so 8x is twice as slow as 4x. Python prototype only: in the plugin the whole amp is oversampled once.

level_db.label: Level
level_db.tooltip: Feedback lowers the volume. Use this to bring it back, so you can compare settings at the same loudness.

ir.label: Cab IR
ir.short: Speaker cabinet sound from an impulse response (.wav) file.
ir.tooltip: An impulse response (IR) is a short recording that captures how a speaker cabinet and microphone change the sound. Loading one makes the amp sound like it is played through that cab. The cab removes the harsh top end of the distortion, so without an IR (or a strong low-pass) a distorted amp sounds buzzy. Put this block last. It adds no delay.

file.label: IR file
file.tooltip: Any mono or stereo .wav file (stereo is mixed to mono). If its sample rate is different from the amp's, it is converted automatically. Most IRs are 20-500 ms long; longer files can include room sound.

mix.label: Mix
mix.short: Blend between no cab (0) and full cab (1).
mix.tooltip: 1 = only the cab sound, the normal setting. Lower values let some of the raw amp signal through, which adds fizz and air. Useful to compare the sound with and without the cab, or to use a direct signal for a special effect.

level_db.label: Level
level_db.tooltip: IR files have very different loudness. Use this to match the volume when switching between cabs, so you hear the tone difference and not the level difference.
